title: Marchfield Public Library - Notes from the Reference Desk
description: The Marchfield Public Library's blog: hours, closures, the Friends' book sale, and Karen Fennimore's notes from the microfilm reader.

data.author: Karen Fennimore
data.tagline: Hours, closures, the book sale, and what is on the microfilm reader.
data.about:
The staff blog of the Marchfield Public Library, 114 Ward Street, Marchfield. Written by Karen Fennimore, archivist since 2004.

Hours, closures and the Friends' book sale go here, and so does anything I find on the microfilm that I have thought about more than once.

The library is scanning the Gridfall Ledger, 1911 to 1998, on one reader, at about eleven pages an hour. Everything scanned is indexed on [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/]the county wiki[/url], free and without an account. The paper's own 1998-2008 site is still up and unmaintained and is the only clean copy of that decade: [url=synth://verityledger.com/]verityledger.com[/url].

The comment box is open. I read all of them. I do not answer most of them any more.

posts.title: Winter hours, and where we are
posts.body:
The building is on winter hours until the first Monday in March, which is the 3rd. Tuesday through Friday ten to six. Saturday ten to two. Closed Sunday and Monday.

The bookdrop is open all the time. It is the slot in the brick by the ramp. It is not the slot by the main door, which is a mail slot, and which people put books in anyway. A book put in the mail slot comes back to us by way of the county mailroom in Gridfall, about nine days later, and it is checked in on the day it arrives.

Microfilm. Reel 178 is finished, which takes us to the end of March 1958. Total since we started in March 2016: 53,600 pages.

It is the same reader. It does about eleven pages an hour on a good day and about eight once the lamp is warm and I have to stop and let it cool. I have asked about a replacement. The answer is that it works, which is true.

Everything scanned is indexed on the county wiki, free, no account: [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/wiki/verity-county]wiki.gridfall.net[/url]. If you want a page and cannot find it there, telephone the reference desk and I will look.

posts.title: A mule on the right of way, June 1923
posts.body:
I am not starting a regular feature. I do not have time for a regular feature. But I have thought about this one twice since Tuesday, so it goes here.

[b]Gridfall Ledger, 12 June 1923, page 4, third column, under the letters.[/b]

A man named E. T. Sarles writes in to say his mule has been on the Verity Rail right of way four times in three weeks, and that this is the railroad's doing because the fence is down at the Kestrel Road culvert. He gives the date of each occasion. He gives the mule's name, which is Prudence. He says he has written to the railroad twice and had no answer, and he asks the paper to print the letter so the railroad will know he is serious.

[b]19 June 1923, page 4.[/b] The Verity Rail superintendent replies. The fence is the landowner's and not the railroad's under the original 1889 conveyance, and he prints the relevant paragraph of it, which is four lines long and settles nothing.

[b]10 July 1923, page 6.[/b] A two-inch item. The fence at the Kestrel Road culvert has been repaired. It does not say by whom.

That is all of it. It took me about eighty pages of scanning to get from the first to the last and it is not important. I liked it.

The rail enthusiasts' board has a thread from 2006 that quotes the same 1889 conveyance in an argument about something else: [url=synth://forums.verityrail.org/]forums.verityrail.org[/url]. The last human post on that board is 2013. It still loads.

comments.author: wpennock
comments.body: The Kestrel Road culvert is still there. It is under the trail now, mile 6.4 measured from the Marchfield end. The headwall is dry stone and there is a date cut into the south face. I have read it as 1889 twice and as 1869 once, in different light.

posts.title: Friends' book sale, Saturday 5 April
posts.body:
Friends of the Library spring sale. Saturday 5 April, nine to two, community room. Doors on the Ward Street side because the ramp is the only way to get a table through.

Hardcovers a dollar. Paperbacks fifty cents. A bag is five dollars and you bring the bag. The bag price starts at noon and not before, and I am putting that in writing because I am asked about it every year by the same four people.

What is in it: about four hundred paperback mysteries out of one estate, most of them read once. The usual run of condensed books that nobody buys and that we put out anyway. A shelf of county and state history. Two boxes of children's picture books in good condition, which will be gone by ten.

What is not in it: the bound Ledger volumes. People ask. They are not ours to sell and they are also in a condition where you would not want them.

Cash. The card reader in the community room stopped working when the building's system was changed over and the vendor says the terminal is out of support. There is a cash box and a person sitting at it.

Money goes to the Friends, and the Friends buy the large print and the audiobooks, which is most of what the Friends have bought for eleven years.

posts.title: Summer reading, the numbers
posts.body:
Summer reading finished on Saturday the 16th. The county asks for the numbers in September and I would rather write them once.

[list][*]Registered: 231. Children and teens together. We stopped splitting them in 2021 because the two-form system confused everybody including us.[*]Completed the programme: 147.[*]Books logged: 4,418.[*]Most logged by one reader: 96. She is nine. Her mother works nights and she was here most mornings from the second week of June. I am not printing her name.[*]Programme events: eleven.[*]Best attended: the reptile man from Halsey, 88 people, which is more people than we have chairs.[*]Least attended: a session on using the online catalogue. Two people, one of whom was staff.[/list]

The prize is a certificate and a bookmark. It has been a certificate and a bookmark since 2016 and nobody has ever complained about it, including the nine-year-old, who took both and asked whether she could start again.

The county also asks for a narrative paragraph. I have written one. It says the programme met its objectives.

posts.title: The reader is down
posts.body:
The microfilm reader stopped on Monday. It is the lamp assembly or it is the board that drives the lamp assembly, and the difference matters, because one of those is a part that still exists.

No scanning until it is fixed. The reels are here and the reading room is open as normal. The second reader still works. It does not scan but it reads, and I will thread it for you, and I will show you how so you can do it yourself next time. People think threading is hard. It is not hard. It is fiddly for about ninety seconds.

I have a service call in. The company that made the machine was bought in 2004 and the company that bought it was bought in 2013, and the number I have now rings at a firm in another state that services four other makes and ours.

Reel 186 is half done. It is September 1959. It will still be September 1959 when the lamp comes back.

posts.title: Five weeks
posts.body:
The reader came back on Tuesday. It was the board, not the lamp.

Five weeks. The part was $312 and the labour was two hours, and the total came in under the threshold that would have required a purchasing process, which is the only reason it happened in five weeks and not in the spring.

Pages scanned in those five weeks: none.

I did the name index back to 1954 instead. It needed doing and I had been putting it off because it is not interesting work. It is done now. If you search the wiki for a surname and it appears in the Ledger between 1954 and 1958, you will get the date and the page number and not just the year.

[url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/wiki/verity-county]The index is here[/url]. There is no account and there is no charge and there never will be, because the day there is, it stops being a library thing.

Reel 186 is finished. October 1959.

posts.title: Mrs. Ordway's boxes
posts.body:
Ruth Ordway brought us four boxes on Tuesday the 2nd. Her husband Carl died in August. He was the county weights and measures inspector from 1971 to 1996, and before that he was at the tannery.

The boxes are his. Not the county's — the county's records are the county's and they are wherever the county put them. These are the ones he kept.

Eleven field notebooks, in pencil, one line per inspection: the date, the business, the scale, whether it passed. Carbon copies of his correspondence, which he kept in order. A run of a departmental newsletter I did not know existed. And four photographs of the tannery yard which I think are 1974, and if anybody can tell me what the long building on the left is, I would like to know.

It is accessioned now. That is the word, and what it means is that somebody in forty years can find it without knowing Carl Ordway's name.

Mrs. Ordway asked whether any of it was worth anything. I said not in money. She said that was fine, she just did not want it in the garage.

It is the best thing anyone has given us this year. The notebooks on their own are a list of every business in this county that had a scale, year by year, for twenty-five years, and that list does not exist anywhere else. Not at the county. I checked.

The tannery article on the wiki is thin and I will be adding to it: [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/wiki/verity-tanning]Verity Tanning[/url].

Thank you.

posts.title: Into 1960
posts.body:
Reel 194 finished Thursday. That is the end of 1960.

Total since March 2016: 58,900 pages.

The paper gets bigger in 1959 and stays bigger through the sixties, so a reel covers less time and a year of paper takes longer. 1958 took about four months. 1960 took five and a half. That is not the machine and it is not me, it is the advertising.

Two things about 1960 that are not findings, just things.

The classified section triples between January and October. Somebody sold a great many cars in Verity County in 1960.

And there is a column called Around the County that runs three times a week, six inches, unsigned. It is entirely who visited whom. Mrs. So-and-so of Coyne Flats spent Sunday with her sister in Halsey. The Pell road crew had a cake for somebody's retirement. It was not news when it was printed and it is not news now.

It is also, if you are trying to establish that a person was alive and in a particular place in October 1960, the only record there is.

posts.title: Closed Monday 9 March
posts.body:
Closed all day Monday 9 March. The community room floor is being refinished and the fumes carry through the whole building, including the stacks.

This has been on the door since January and on the county calendar since January. I am putting it here as well because the county calendar is not a thing anybody reads, and because the last time we closed for a day, four people drove in from Coyne Flats.

Bookdrop open as usual. Anything that comes in Monday is checked in Tuesday morning and nothing is overdue because of it.

Holds that arrive Monday will be on the shelf Tuesday by eleven.

The Friends' sale is the Saturday after, 14 March, and it is not affected. The floor will have been walked on for five days by then.

posts.title: The library's annual report, 1934
posts.body:
A woman came in Tuesday wanting her grandmother's wedding announcement. August 1934. We found it: 18 August 1934, page 3, four inches, and it lists what everybody wore.

While the reel was on I read the facing page, which is what happens, and page 2 of that issue is this library's annual report to the county.

[list][*]Circulation for the year: 14,206 volumes.[*]Registered borrowers: 1,918, in a town of about four thousand.[*]Expenditure on books: $211.40.[*]The librarian is named. Miss Agnes Weill. Her salary is printed, because they printed it then. $780 for the year.[/list]

There is one paragraph of commentary at the end and it says that demand for fiction remains high and that the Board would prefer it were otherwise.

Our circulation last year was 31,400. Our materials budget was $9,400. The Board has no commentary.

Agnes Weill is in the 1940 and 1946 reports as well and not in the 1949 one, and there is nothing in between that I have found, which means she either left or she did not and somebody stopped printing it.

posts.title: Into 1962
posts.body:
Reel 203 is finished. We are into 1962.

Total since March 2016: 60,700 pages.

Somebody asked on AskVerity on the 5th where you can read a Verity County newspaper from before 2000, and I wrote it out there: [url=synth://askverity.com/q/q-17]the question is here[/url]. It was closed as a duplicate of a question about records request forms, which is a different question with a different answer. The answer is still on the page and the page still loads, so it is fine.

Somebody else asked me at the desk in April when this will be finished, and I did the arithmetic that evening and have not put it anywhere until now.

1963 to 1998 is about 75,000 pages at the rate the paper ran. Against what I actually get through in a year — and I used the last three years, not a good year — that is 2038.

I will be seventy.

Reel 204 is on the machine.

posts.title: Three hundred and thirty-one
posts.body:
The county wiki has an article about the 2003 substation fire. It gives the date as 11 June 2003. It gives the cause as the state utility commission's November 2003 finding, insulation degradation consistent with age. It gives the toll as nobody killed and two Gridfall volunteer firefighters treated at County General for smoke inhalation and released the same afternoon.

All three of those are what the Ledger printed on 12 June 2003, page 1, four columns and a photograph of the fence line at Depot and Quarry. I have scanned that page and it is cited on the article. The commission summary is two pages and it is cited as well.

[url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/wiki/substation-fire-2003]The article is here.[/url]

Since 9 February 2023, edits have come in that change 2003 to 2004. Sometimes the cause to lightning. Sometimes the toll to two dead. Most often all three in one edit, with a summary saying the article has been updated for accuracy.

I revert them. The count in my spreadsheet this morning is 331.

They come from different accounts. None of those accounts has edited anything else, on any article. The edit summaries are not identical but they are the same three or four sentences in a different order.

9 February 2023 is when I started counting. It is not when it started. I do not know when it started.

The paper's own current site says 2004: [url=synth://now.verityledger.com/article/a-02]here[/url]. It is the same paper.

The utility's announcements page mentions the fire once, on the twentieth anniversary: [url=synth://vvpl.news/post/twenty-years-2023]here[/url]. It is four hundred words. It gives the date correctly and it does not say what caused it.

The page is on my watchlist and I look at it in the morning while the reel loads, which takes four minutes.

It is correct as of this morning.

The toll came off County General on the telephone from a charge nurse whose name is in my notebook, and I called back an hour later and got it a second time because the first number I was given was wrong. That is two phone calls. It took eleven minutes.

posts.title: Reel 205 is not 1963
posts.body:
Reel 205 should be January to June 1963. It is May to October 1974.

The vendor filmed this collection in 1983 and 1984 and typed an index card for every reel. The card for 205 says 1963. The leader on the reel says 1974, in the same typing, and the frames say 1974 as well, so the reel is not mislabelled. The card is.

I checked 206 and 207 before I did anything else. 206 is 1963 from January. 207 is 1963 from July. So it is one reel out of place and not a whole run, which is the good version of this.

I scanned 205 anyway. It was threaded, and it is 1974 whether I scan it now or in twelve years, and somebody will want it. So we are into 1974, technically. We are also still at 1962.

Where 1974's own reel is, I do not know. The numbering runs 1 to 291 with no gap in it, which means there is a reel somewhere in the seventies that is going to turn out to be something else when I get there.

I have written to the vendor. The vendor stopped existing in 1994. I have written to the company that bought the company that bought them, and I have an acknowledgement with a ticket number, and that is where that is.

1974 is a good year to have early, as it happens. The Ledger goes to offset in March and the photographs stop being grey.

comments.author: kfennimore
comments.body: Only one caught, because I only check the card against the leader when something looks wrong, and until Monday nothing had. I am going to pull every tenth card and check it against the leader, which is 29 reels and about two hours, and I will put the result here.

posts.title: What a deposit is
posts.body:
People bring things in, ask whether we want them, apologise, and then start explaining why it is probably not worth anything. You can skip that part. Here is what actually happens.

You bring it to the reference desk. Paper, photographs, a disc, a cassette, a ledger, a scrapbook, a box you have not opened. I look at it with you and I write down what you know about it while you are standing there, because what you know about it is half of what it is, and once you have gone out of the door I cannot get it back.

Then it gets a number, a folder and a line in the finding aid. That is an accession, and what it buys you is that in forty years somebody who never heard of you can find it.

What we cannot take. Anything that needs a climate-controlled room, because we do not have one and I will tell you who does. Anything with a condition attached that I cannot honestly keep. Anything that is really the county's, because the county's records have a place and it is not here.

What is in the local collection now:

[list][*]The Gridfall Ledger on microfilm, 1911 to 1998. Complete except four months of 1943 where the film is damaged.[*]Blue Kestrel material, copied for us by Marion Teale. Menus, the booth map, the 1977 kitchen fire.[*]Walt Pennock's reception logs, 2019 to date, deposited annually, on paper and on disc.[*]A disc of the Gridfall boards through 2012 that Dale Carver made and brought in without being asked.[*]Carl Ordway's papers.[*]About eleven boxes that came in without explanation, which is why I ask.[/list]

Marion's site is still up and is better than anything I could write about the diner: [url=synth://kestrel-journal.net/]kestrel-journal.net[/url]. It has not been updated since 2019 and it does not need to be.

Hours are on the door, and on [url=synth://verity.county.gov/]the county site[/url], where they are wrong. Ours are right.

comments.body: Bring the cookbook. Church and grange cookbooks are the best list of who lived where in a year that exists, because every recipe has a name under it and the names are in order by street. Keep the cards. Photograph them if you want and bring the photographs.
